Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you make this into one standalone fictional episode, set at a ferry luggage desk, not a general description of how ferry desks work. i want the episode to stay with one late-afternoon shift and feel like something happening in a real terminal. the desk is at Alder Quay, and the ferry is the Bracken, sailing to Larkhaven. it is a weekday, the rain has just eased, and the departure is at 18:20. when the clerk first looks up at the wall clock it is 17:55, so there is time pressure but not a last-second emergency. use connected paragraphs, with enough ordinary detail about the desk and the queue that the place feels lived in. don't turn the scene into an adventure or a big crisis.

Jo is working the desk. Jo has a habit of smoothing the corners of claim slips before writing on them, and there is a small desk lamp with a green shade even though the overhead lights are on. the counter has a low brass rail, and a laminated card explains that loose baggage has to be entered before it can go into the loading area. those details can come through while Jo is doing the work rather than being listed as an introduction. there is a damp patch on the floor by the entrance from people coming in out of the rain. a cleaner has put a yellow cone beside it, but the cone is slightly off to one side, so people are walking around it in different ways. keep the room busy without making the crowd enormous.

the main luggage problem concerns one navy-blue hard-sided suitcase with a red webbing strap. the suitcase has a small brass tag on its handle and a claim stub numbered 481. the recipient instruction for that case must say “Saskia, not Ellis”. keep that exact distinction clear whenever the recipient is mentioned: the case is for Saskia, not Ellis. Ellis is also in the scene, but Ellis is waiting to ask about a missing wool scarf, a separate matter. don't make Ellis the suitcase recipient or suggest that the claim stub changes who the case is for. Saskia has come to the desk to check that the suitcase has been entered correctly; don't give Saskia a surname or add a personal history.

Jo has to compare the number on the stub with the number entered on the desk sheet, look at the red strap, and confirm the recipient wording. use those details in the order that makes sense in the interaction, not as a block of technical instructions. one brief numbered section would fit naturally as a copied portion of Jo's checking list, with these three items in this order: claim number, red strap, recipient. it should look like something a clerk might actually write down during a busy shift, not like a formal report pasted into a story. include the exact stub number, 481, and don't silently change the luggage description or the names.

there are two other people in the queue who can help make the desk feel occupied: a parent holding a green duffel while a child keeps asking whether the ferry has a snack counter, and a courier with a folded hand trolley who needs to know where to leave a parcel for the loading crew. the parent has already folded a paper timetable into quarters, and the courier keeps one hand on the trolley handle while talking. keep their questions brief and let Jo respond as part of the same shift. they are not the focus, and their baggage should not get mixed up with the navy suitcase or with Ellis's scarf question. don't add a new passenger who takes over the episode.

include an ordinary spoken quote, not a slogan or a dramatic speech. something Saskia says while Jo is checking the entry could be “The red strap is under the side handle.” use that wording as Saskia's quote. let the line sit naturally in the exchange, with a short response or action from Jo around it. no one should explain the whole plot aloud. the tone should be observant and calm, with small signs of hurry in the queue and in the approaching sailing, but not panic. the rain, the clock and the ferry timetable can be noticed in passing rather than repeated in every paragraph.

keep the practical handling of the case visible: Jo needs the desk sheet, the claim stub and the luggage tag, and the laminated card about entering loose baggage before it goes to the loading area can matter to the moment. do not introduce a new rule about payment, identification or security. the suitcase is still at the luggage desk during the scene; don't move it onto the ferry or decide what happens to it after the check. keep the distinction between checking an entry and physically loading a case. nobody needs to resolve Ellis's scarf question in this episode, and the courier's parcel can remain a separate desk matter. don't add a conclusion that says all problems are solved.

there can be small concrete movements: Jo turning the stub toward the lamp, Saskia shifting position to see the sheet, or the parent guiding the child around the damp patch. use only what helps the moment, and don't stack these gestures in every sentence. keep the names consistent and don't give anyone extra relationships or motives. the desk sheet is a working sheet, not a public notice, and claim stub 481 belongs to the navy suitcase with the red strap. the scene should remain one continuous episode at Alder Quay, rather than jumping to the ferry or to another day.

end with a final paragraph that brings in distinct information rather than repeating the suitcase check or summarizing the scene. the departure board also lists a 20:05 ferry to West Reach, and its small printed note says that bicycles must be brought to the side gate before boarding. that later sailing is not the Bracken's 18:20 trip to Larkhaven. you can let one of the people notice the board or let Jo see it from the desk, but keep the two departures distinct. write a complete episode with a natural ending, while leaving the actual outcome of the suitcase check unspecified.", "output": "Write one standalone fictional episode at the luggage desk at Alder Quay. Keep the scene within a single weekday late-afternoon shift and use connected paragraphs with concrete details. The Bracken is due to sail to Larkhaven at 18:20. Jo first looks at the wall clock at 17:55, creating mild time pressure but no last-second emergency. The rain has just eased, and the terminal is busy without being crowded. Keep the tone observant and calm; do not turn the scene into an adventure or a crisis.

Show Jo working at the desk through the action rather than presenting a list of introductory details. Jo smooths the corners of claim slips before writing. A green-shaded desk lamp sits beneath the overhead lights; a low brass rail runs along the counter; and a laminated card explains that loose baggage must be entered before it can go into the loading area. Near the entrance, a yellow cleaning cone stands slightly to one side of a damp floor patch, and people navigate around it differently. Let the clock, rain, and timetable appear in passing rather than repeating them in every paragraph.

The main luggage matter is a navy-blue hard-sided suitcase with a red webbing strap, a small brass tag on its handle, and claim stub 481. Saskia comes to check that the suitcase has been entered correctly. The recipient instruction must read exactly “Saskia, not Ellis.” Keep that distinction clear whenever the recipient is mentioned: the case is for Saskia, not Ellis. Do not give Saskia a surname or personal history. Ellis is also present, but is waiting to ask about a missing wool scarf; that is separate from the suitcase. Do not make Ellis the recipient or imply that the claim stub changes who the case is for.

Show Jo comparing the stub number with the number on the desk sheet, looking at the red strap, and confirming the recipient wording, in an order that fits the interaction. Include a brief numbered section as a copied portion of Jo’s checking list, with these three items in this order:
1. Claim number
2. Red strap
3. Recipient

Make the list look like something a clerk might write during a busy shift, not a formal report inserted into the story. Keep the exact stub number, 481, and do not change the luggage description or names. Jo needs the desk sheet, claim stub, and luggage tag. The laminated card may matter to the moment, but do not introduce new rules about payment, identification, or security. The suitcase remains at the desk during the scene: do not move it onto the ferry or decide what happens to it after the check. Keep checking an entry distinct from physically loading a case. Leave Ellis’s scarf question unresolved and keep the courier’s parcel separate. Do not conclude that all problems are solved.

Include two other people in the queue, briefly and as part of the same shift. A parent holds a green duffel while a child repeatedly asks whether the ferry has a snack counter; the parent has folded a paper timetable into quarters. A courier with a folded hand trolley needs to know where to leave a parcel for the loading crew and keeps one hand on the trolley handle while talking. Let Jo respond to their questions, but keep them secondary. Do not mix their belongings up with the navy suitcase or Ellis’s scarf, and do not add another passenger who takes over the episode.

Include this ordinary spoken quote from Saskia while Jo checks the entry: “The red strap is under the side handle.” Let it sit naturally in the exchange, with a short response or action from Jo. Avoid slogans, dramatic speeches, and explanations of the whole plot spoken aloud. Small movements such as Jo turning the stub toward the lamp, Saskia shifting to see the sheet, or the parent guiding the child around the damp patch may be used where they help. Do not overload the scene with gestures. Keep names consistent, add no extra relationships or motives, and keep the desk sheet a working sheet rather than a public notice.

Keep the episode continuous at Alder Quay; do not jump to the ferry or another day. End with a final paragraph containing distinct information rather than a recap of the suitcase check. The departure board also lists a 20:05 ferry to West Reach, and a small printed note says bicycles must be brought to the side gate before boarding. Keep that sailing distinct from the Bracken’s 18:20 trip to Larkhaven. Jo or one of the people may notice the board. Give the episode a natural ending, but leave the actual outcome of the suitcase check unspecified."}]
